# Section 6 - Procedures
## Part A - Supporting Academic Integrity 
(12)  The University supports the maintenance of academic integrity throughout the University community, including where partners are involved in teaching La Trobe courses, through:
  1. the operations of a dedicated Academic Integrity Unit (AIU). The functions of the AIU are to: 
    1. support the promotion of academic integrity;
    2. provide process support for allegations of academic misconduct;
    3. maintain all records associated with allegations;
    4. provide regular reporting of academic misconduct allegations and trends to university committees; and
    5. co-design academic integrity initiatives with students, including student representatives.
  2. the appointment and training of at least three Academic Integrity Advisors (AIA) per school. AIAs act as the main point of contact for academic integrity matters and receive referrals for and investigate allegations of academic misconduct within and between schools;
  3. the requirement for staff and students to undertake academic integrity training;
  4. the provision of specifically designed academic integrity support and development resources for students;
  5. the provision of dedicated resources for staff including: 
    1. guidance in the design of assessment to reduce the risk of academic misconduct;
    2. suggested learning activities to embed in the curriculum to promote awareness of academic integrity; and
    3. professional development and resources to support the identification of different types of academic misconduct, especially contract cheating and the inappropriate use of artificial intelligence.
  6. the establishment of a Student Academic Misconduct Committee (SAMC) to investigate and determine allegations of Serious Academic Misconduct; and
  7. the adoption of specific measures to reduce the incidence of cheating including: 
    1. the blocking of access to contract cheating services through the University network;
    2. specific advice to students about avoiding any contact with such services;
    3. monitoring the emergence of relevant material on contract cheating sites, issuing alerts to staff and working to have such content removed where possible; and
    4. guidance to students about the appropriate use of artificial intelligence.


(13)  The respective Academic Integrity Modules (AIM) for staff and students must be successfully completed as follows:
  1. staff are required to complete the staff AIM during their induction; and
  2. students are required to complete the student AIM before the end of their first teaching period of their course. Students returning to study from a period of exclusion due to academic misconduct are required to complete the AIM again before the end of the first teaching period after re-admission.


(14)  Where students do not complete the AIM within the designated time period:
  1. sanctions will be placed on the release of their official results and their access to results; and
  2. they cannot be deemed to have completed the requirements of their course until the AIM has been completed.


(15)  Students taking subjects as part of VCE or a pathway program are encouraged to complete AIM. Failure to complete the module will not result in sanctions unless the requirement to do so is part of a penalty applied under this Policy.
## Part B - Recordkeeping and Confidentiality
(16)  The University maintains a secure database through which all student academic misconduct allegations and associated evidence are submitted and records are kept, in accordance with the University’s [Records Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=10). The AIU collects and retains the following summary information:
  1. information relating to the allegation and investigation: 
    1. the student and the course in which the student is enrolled at the time of the allegation;
    2. a summary of the allegation; and
    3. who carried out the investigation and details regarding meetings held.
  2. information in relation to findings: 
    1. which of the possible findings has been determined (No Case To Answer [including Poor Academic Practice], Minor, or Serious Academic Misconduct);
    2. the factors taken into consideration;
    3. the information on which the decision is based;
    4. the outcome and reasons for the outcome; and
    5. outcomes of any appeals lodged in relation to the findings of an investigation.


(17)  The AIU notifies students against whom an allegation has been made of the outcome of any determination (and any penalty as applicable), and relevant staff as outlined in each stage of this Procedure.
(18)  Where a penalty includes suspension, exclusion, or revocation of an award, the action takes effect on the date of the notification of outcome or at the conclusion of any appeal that may be lodged, whichever is the later.
(19)  Apart from designated relevant staff, all information associated with an allegation remains confidential and is only used for the purpose for which it was provided, unless:
  1. the student gives their express consent in writing;
  2. the information gives the University grounds for concern about the security of people or property;
  3. procedural fairness requires the information to be shared;
  4. access to the information is required by law;
  5. the University is obliged or able to do so under the University’s [Privacy Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=1); and
  6. such information is required by regulators, government agencies (eg, TEQSA, the current Commonwealth department responsible for education [especially in relation to international students], Auditor-General’s Department, professional bodies, or sponsors of international students.


(20)  If a student appeals the outcome of a decision made under the [Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36) and the matter proceeds to the University Appeals Committee, the University Appeals Committee will have access to:
  1. the information regarding the initial investigation;
  2. any information associated with the SAMC meeting (if undertaken); and
  3. summary details of any cases of academic misconduct recorded for that student (including cases where there was a finding that no misconduct occurred).


(21)  Students may seek access to any information held by the University about allegations of academic misconduct against them by contacting the AIU.
## Part C - Initial Management of Allegations
### Identification of Suspected Academic Misconduct
(22)  Suspected academic misconduct may be identified by staff, students, or external sources.
(23)  The University uses various methods to identify academic misconduct, including:
  1. work submitted by students for assessment may be checked using text, code, or other comparative software, or manually reviewed using web search engines, checking of student sources, comparison with other assignments, and consultation with colleagues; and
  2. information in the [Learning Management System (LMS)](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=338&version=1&associated) about the submission may be compared with activity or access logs.


### Reporting of Allegations and Collation of Evidence
(24)  All individuals who identify a case of suspected academic misconduct in any academic work other than an examination must submit a report with evidence to the AIU as soon as practicable, allowing for the time required to gather appropriate evidence. This should normally be within five (5) business days of the issue being identified, or no later than four (4) weeks from the submission date of the assessment task. Reports submitted outside these timeframes must be accompanied by a reason for the delay.
(25)  The different types of academic misconduct that may be referred are as follows:  
| Academic Misconduct Type  | Description of Suspected Student Action  |  
| --- | --- |  
| 
#### Supervised Assessment (including exams)
 |   |  
| Cheating  | fails to comply with any reasonable direction relating to conduct in supervised assessments (which may or may not include inappropriate use of AI)  |  
| 
#### Any Assessment Type (supervised or unsupervised)
 |   |  
| Cheating – Other  | fails to comply with any reasonable direction relating to academic conduct or any other academic misconduct not listed that provides the student with an unjustified or unfair advantage  |  
| Collusion  | colludes or attempts to collude with another student to prepare assessment work that was intended to be completed individually, either deliberately or by not taking reasonable care to protect their own work  |  
| Contract Cheating  | outsources all or part of their assessment to a third party (which may or may not include a commercial provider, AI, current or former student, family member or acquaintance, paid or unpaid). It includes organising another person to take any assessment in place of the intended student  |  
| Contract Cheating – File Sharing Sites  | uploads any student work or copyright material to a file-sharing website that allows anyone to download the documents, or accesses such a site with a view to gain access to any documents that may or may not provide academic advantage to the student  |  
| Fabrication  | fabricates any information and/or references in any assessment submission – which may or may not include references fabricated as a result of the use of AI  |  
| Falsification  | tampers with any documents or misrepresents information related to any assessment or application to the University that leads to academic advantage  |  
| Plagiarism  | uses ideas, concepts, words, or structures without appropriately acknowledging the source(even if the source is AI)  |  
| Self-Plagiarism  | presents text, ideas or data from their own previous submitted scholarly work without written permission from the Subject Coordinator  
 |  
(26)  All allegations undergo a preliminary assessment by the AIU to determine that sufficient documentation has been provided to allow the allegation to be properly investigated. All reports are submitted to the relevant AIA, with the following exceptions:
  1. allegations from external sources are submitted directly to the SAMC; and
  2. following a preliminary investigation by the AIU, allegations against graduates of the University are notified to the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) (DVCA) for management under the provisions of the [Degrees, Diplomas and other Awards Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=90).


(27)  An individual who has submitted a report to the AIU may apply to withdraw the report where relevant subsequent information becomes available. The withdrawal of a report can only occur prior to any notification being made to the student, and with the approval of the Director, Integrity Office.
(28)  Where the alleged misconduct takes place in an examination, the Chief Invigilator records all details in an Examination Misconduct Report and submits the report to the Deputy Director, Academic Services or nominee (see [Assessment Procedure - Examinations](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=338)) who then submits a copy of the report to the AIU as soon as possible for referral to the appropriate AIA.
(29)  The complete portfolio of evidence compiled for all allegations may include:
  1. the Subject Learning Guide and any other contextual information where it is not included in the Guide, such as the assessment design, submission method, and any academic integrity materials or instruction provided in the subject;
  2. the assessment task;
  3. any results from the use of text or code comparative software (with the exception of artificial intelligence detection software), plagiarism detection software, or web search engines;
  4. outcomes from any review of the sources cited by the student, comparison with other assignments, and consultation with other relevant academic staff;
  5. any discipline-specific information regarding the case; and
  6. any additional evidence gathered, including but not limited to evidence of student learning and access to university systems (inclusive of that found through detection tools embedded within learning platforms), emails, texts/messaging and social media posts.


(30)  The portfolio of evidence is accompanied by supplementary information where there are any other prior or current allegations recorded for the student (for any course of enrolment). The allegation at hand is investigated on the basis of the available evidence for that allegation only; however, any supplementary information may be used to facilitate discussions with the student about their overall studies and progress, or to determine an appropriate penalty.
(31)  In assembling and considering the portfolio of evidence, the AIA, SAMC, or AIU is permitted to:
  1. request further information from the Subject Coordinator, according to the guidance provided in the [Guidelines for Managing and Investigating Student Misconduct Allegations](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0016/341512/Guidelines-for-Managing-and-Investigating-Student-Academic-Misconduct-Allegations-2024.pdf) (staff only);
  2. request records of student access to relevant University computerised systems including times, locations, and related information; and
  3. seek information from any relevant person.


## Part D - AIA-Led Investigations
### Initial Review 
(32)  Having reviewed the available evidence an AIA may make any of the following initial determinations:
  1. the allegation lacks sufficient evidence to warrant further investigation. In this case the AIA will direct that: 
    1. the report be dismissed;
    2. the relevant work be accepted for marking; and
    3. the Subject Coordinator and the person who made the allegation be provided with a written outcome of their determination.
  2. the report contains sufficient evidence of Poor Academic Practice or Minor Academic Misconduct to warrant further investigation. In this case an investigation will proceed; and
  3. the report contains sufficient evidence of Serious Academic Misconduct to warrant referral to SAMC. In this case the AIA refers the case, with any outcomes of their initial review, to the AIU. The AIU then refers the allegation and accompanying evidence to the SAMC and advises the student (see Part E).


### Communication With Students
(33)  Where the AIA determines to proceed with an investigation, they direct the AIU to notify the student of the allegation. This is done in writing via the student’s University email account, or last known address in the case of former students, as soon as practicable and within ten (10) business days of receiving a report. The email uses the standard Notification Letter and: 
  1. provides information about the alleged academic misconduct;
  2. advises of a date for an online meeting no less than five (5) business days from the date of the Notification Letter, and informs the student that they may also respond to the allegation in writing (students may request an extension to the date where required);
  3. includes a link to this Policy and its associated documents;
  4. includes a copy of the portfolio of evidence provided to the AIA and any supplementary information;
  5. offers an opportunity for the student to provide any relevant additional information; and
  6. advises the student of their right to have a support person at the meeting and provides information about relevant University support services.


(34)  If the student agrees to participate in a meeting with the AIA, they are entitled to be accompanied to any meeting by a support person. The support person may be any person, including disability support worker or a student advocate from a student association. The support person may not be any person who has a law degree or who is a legal practitioner. The support person may not represent or advocate for the student unless permitted by the AIA.
(35)  The student should respond as soon as practicable but must respond within five (5) business days of the issue of the Notification Letter and advise:
  1. whether they will attend the meeting and/or if they will respond to the allegation in writing; and
  2. if they are to attend the meeting whether they will be accompanied by a support person and the identity of that person.


(36)  Where a student chooses to respond to the allegation in writing, their response should be submitted at least 24 hours before the scheduled day and time of the meeting.
### Investigations
(37)  Where a meeting is held, a member of professional or academic staff may attend as an administrative officer, or for training purposes with the consent of the student. A written record of the meeting must be made and submitted to the AIU.
(38)  The AIA may determine the outcome in the absence of a response from the student.
(39)  During their investigation, the AIA is permitted to speak to any person they consider might help them to reach a decision.
### Outcomes of Investigations
(40)  After consideration of the evidence, the AIA makes one of the following determinations, as close as possible to the date of the scheduled meeting:
  1. No Case to Answer – no academic misconduct has occurred for one of the following reasons: 
    1. there is insufficient evidence to support, on the balance of probabilities, a finding of academic misconduct. The AIA will direct that the work be marked and no further action be taken; or
    2. the incident is a result of Poor Academic Practice. The AIA will direct that the work be marked and that the student be provided with academic counselling or other educative options from the [Schedule](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=387&version=3&associated).
  2. Minor Academic Misconduct – there is sufficient evidence to support, on the balance of probabilities, a finding of Minor Academic Misconduct. The AIA will direct that a minor penalty and educative action be applied according to the options available in the [Schedule](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=387&version=3&associated).
  3. Serious Academic Misconduct – there is sufficient evidence of Serious Academic Misconduct to warrant referral to the SAMC.


(41)  Within ten (10) business days of the AIA making their decision the AIU ensures that:
  1. the student (via their University email account), the Subject Coordinator, and the staff member (but not member of public or student) who submitted the original allegation are provided with a written outcome of the AIAs determination including: 
    1. their findings;
    2. a summary of the evidence on which those findings are based;
    3. any actions or penalties that were determined;
    4. a brief statement of reasons;
    5. the details of how and where the student may appeal the decision and/or penalty and within what timeframe; and
    6. information regarding available support services.
  2. appropriate records are stored;
  3. the Director of Student Advising (for international student support and advice)and the Pro Vice-Chancellor (Recruitment and International Operations) or their nominees are notified where the student is an international student and any penalty imposed could have consequences for the student’s visa.


(42)  The Subject Coordinator, or the relevant assessor, is responsible for ensuring that any relevant actions or penalties specified in the outcome are applied in a timely manner in order to facilitate timely results processing and release in accordance with the assurance of results provisions in the [Assessment Procedure - Validation and Moderation](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=140).
## Part E - Cases Referred to the Student Academic Misconduct Committee
### Referral
(43)  Cases are referred to the SAMC by the AIU:
  1. directly, where the allegation has been reported by a source external to the University; and
  2. following a referral by an AIA where, after a preliminary investigation the evidence appears to indicate Serious Academic Misconduct may have occurred.


(44)  The AIU ensures that referred reports are accompanied by a comprehensive portfolio of evidence, including any supplementary information and the outcomes of any initial investigations by the relevant AIA.
### Communication with Students
(45)  When it is determined that a case is to be referred to the SAMC, the AIU sends a SAMC Notification Letter to the student via their University email account, or last known address in the case of former students, as soon as practicable and at least ten (10) business days before the SAMC is due to meet. The email:
  1. provides information about the alleged academic misconduct;
  2. requests that the student attend the online meeting of the Committee in person and informs the student that they may also respond to the allegation in writing;
  3. includes a copy of the portfolio of evidence to be provided to the Committee, and any supplementary information;
  4. includes a link to this Policy and associated documents;
  5. offers the student an opportunity to provide any relevant additional information;
  6. advises the student of their right to have any relevant support person at the meeting; and
  7. provides the student with information about relevant University support services.


(46)  If the student agrees to participate in a meeting with the SAMC, they are entitled to be accompanied to any meeting by a support person. The support person may be any person, including a disability worker or a student advocate from a student association. The support person may not be any person who has a law degree or who is a legal practitioner. The support person may not represent or advocate for the student unless permitted by the SAMC.
(47)  The student should respond as soon as practicable but must respond within ten (10) business days of the issue of the SAMC Notification Letter. When responding to the request to attend the meeting, the student must advise:
  1. whether they will attend a meeting and/or respond to the allegation in writing; and
  2. if they are to attend a meeting whether they will be accompanied by a support person and the identity of that person.


(48)  If the student does not respond to the SAMC Notification Letter within ten (10) business days, the SAMC meeting will proceed in their absence.
### Conduct of the Student Academic Misconduct Committee Meeting
(49)  The membership of the SAMC is as required in the [Terms of Reference](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0030/289821/SAMC-Terms-of-Reference_Aug-2022.pdf) (staff only). The SAMC is supported by a member of professional staff from the AIU.
(50)  The SAMC has access to the portfolio of evidence compiled by the AIU.
(51)  The members of the SAMC are responsible for maintaining the confidentiality of third parties where required when documents are circulated.
(52)  The Chair of the SAMC is permitted to speak to any person they consider might help the Committee reach a decision.
### Outcomes of a SAMC Meeting
(53)  After consideration of the evidence the SAMC makes one of the following determinations:
  1. No Case to Answer - no academic misconduct has occurred for either one of the following reasons: 
    1. there is insufficient evidence to support, on the balance of probabilities, a finding of academic misconduct. The SAMC will direct that the work be marked and no further action be taken; or
    2. the incident is a result of Poor Academic Practice. The SAMC will refer the matter back to the relevant AIA for the application of academic counselling or other educative options from the [Schedule](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=387&version=3&associated).
  2. Minor Academic Misconduct – there is sufficient evidence to support, on the balance of probabilities, a finding of Minor Academic Misconduct. The SAMC will refer the matter back to the relevant AIA for the application of a penalty and appropriate actions according to the options available in the [Schedule](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=387&version=3&associated);
  3. Serious Academic Misconduct – there is sufficient evidence to support, on the balance of probabilities, a finding of Serious Academic Misconduct. The SAMC will direct that one or more penalties for Serious Academic Misconduct be applied, and an educative response where appropriate, according to the options available in the [Schedule](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=387&version=3&associated).


(54)  In some cases, the matter may also be referred by the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) to TEQSA, police and/or other relevant authorities, or to another area of the University for managing under other policies such as the [Student Conduct Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382).
(55)  Within ten (10) business days of the SAMC meeting the AIU: 
  1. provides to the student (via their University email account), the Subject Coordinator, and the staff member (but not a member of the public or student) who submitted the original allegation a written outcome including: 
    1. the findings;
    2. a summary of the evidence on which those findings are based;
    3. any educative actions and/or penalties to be applied;
    4. a brief statement of reasons;
    5. the details of how and where the student may appeal the decision and/or a penalty and within what timeframe; and
    6. information regarding available support services.
  2. ensures appropriate records are stored;
  3. as applicable, notifies the following: 
    1. the Director, Academic Services, or their nominee, where a penalty includes suspension or exclusion;
    2. the relevant Course Coordinator(s);
    3. the Director, Student Advising (for international support and advice);
    4. the Pro Vice-Chancellor (Recruitment and International Operations) or their nominee where the student is an international student and any penalty imposed could have consequences for the student’s visa; and
    5. the relevant Academic Integrity Advisor.


(56)  The Subject Coordinator, or the relevant assessor, is responsible for ensuring that any actions or penalties specified in the outcome are applied in a timely manner in order to assist the student and to facilitate timely results processing and release in accordance with the assurance of results provisions in the [Assessment Procedure - Validation and Moderation](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=140).
## Part F - Appeals
(57)  Students may appeal a determination of minor or serious academic misconduct made under this Policy, including any penalty, within twenty (20) business days of receiving the notice of decision. Appeals must be lodged in writing with the University Appeals Committee (UAC), accompanied by appropriate evidence, and can only be made where the student can demonstrate that:
  1. this Policy and Procedure were not appropriately followed in the reaching of the determination or penalty; or
  2. there was bias towards the student on the part of any individual involved with the findings; or
  3. more evidence has become available that was not available to decision-makers at the time.


(58)  Where a penalty is suspension or exclusion, no action may be taken to implement the penalty associated with an allegation before:
  1. the conclusion of the 20-day appeal period, even if the student has not yet lodged an appeal; and
  2. the UAC has completed its review and issued its findings, where the student has lodged a timely appeal against any penalty.


(59)  The decision of the UAC is the final decision of the University. The University Ombudsman is not able to review decisions made by the UAC, however students who have concerns about any aspect of the process or the way in which this Policy has been applied (as opposed to the decision or outcome) may lodge a complaint with the Office of the University Ombudsman.
(60)  Students who remain dissatisfied after all University processes have been exhausted may choose to lodge a complaint with the [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated).
## Part G - Quality Assurance and Governance
(61)  Data on academic misconduct is monitored at each subject review and any required actions are included in subject action plans as outlined in the [Course and Subject Management Procedure - Monitoring and Review](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=386). Academic misconduct data for third-party teaching partners is reviewed through annual reporting and overseen by the relevant Joint Management Committee.
(62)  All data collected on academic misconduct in learning and teaching activities is monitored and analysed by the Director, Integrity Office. Reports comprising de-identified data are:
  1. generated quarterly for internal monitoring; and
  2. submitted to Education Committee once a year for oversight and monitoring of trends across the University, prior to submission to Academic Board.


(63)  Copies of all reports are provided to schools to inform curriculum and local improvements.

# Section 7 - Definitions
(64)  For the purposes of this Policy and Procedure:
  1. academic integrity: being honest in academic work and taking responsibility for learning and implementing the conventions of scholarship.
  2. academic misconduct: according to Section 1 of the [Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36) academic misconduct includes: 
    1. cheating, plagiarism or any other conduct engaged in by a student with a view to gaining for himself, herself, themself or another person an unfair or unjustified advantage in a formal examination or assessment or in relation to or for a formal examination or assessment, whether such advantage occurs or not (cheating means cheating in relation to a formal examination or assessment and includes a failure to comply with any reasonable direction or instruction of an officer, employee or agent of the University relating to the conduct of the formal examination or assessment);
    2. conduct which constitutes a breach of any rules relating to a formal examination or assessment;
    3. conduct engaged in by a student with a view to gaining for himself, herself, themself or another person an unfair or unjustified advantage in relation to any other requirements of a course or subject, including without limitation class attendance or participation requirements and requirements pertaining to placements, whether such advantage occurs or not; and 
    4. any prescribed conduct.
  3. artificial intelligence: a machine-based system or application that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments. Different AI systems vary in their levels of autonomy and adaptiveness after deployment. (Source: OECD 2023) See the OECD Explanatory memorandum on the updated OECD definition of an AI system | OECD Artificial Intelligence Papers | OECD iLibrary (oecd-ilibrary.org) for explanatory material about the definition.
  4. business day: a day upon which the University is open for business.
  5. exclusion: the temporary or permanent prohibition of an individual from accessing any or all University facilities and services or participating in University activities. A temporary prohibition may be for a specific period or until a condition or conditions have been met. Where a student or participant is excluded from a course, short course or subject, their enrolment in the course, short course or subject is cancelled, and where not prevented by the terms of their exclusion, they must reapply for admission.
  6. Minor Academic Misconduct: academic misconduct which, in all the circumstances, falls short of serious academic misconduct ([Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36)).
  7. natural justice: procedural fairness. The principle of natural justice as applied to this Policy means: 
    1. students are provided with copies of all relevant evidence that has been submitted for an allegation and links to all relevant policies and schedules prior to any meeting or hearing being conducted; and
    2. students are entitled to have a fair and impartial hearing and to make written and/or oral submissions on their behalf.
  8. Plain English: language that aligns with the University’s Brand and Editorial Style Guide and the [Student Communications Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212) that is easily understood by a diverse audience.
  9. Poor Academic Practice: inappropriate academic practice that is judged not to be academic misconduct. A finding of Poor Academic Practice is a possible outcome from the initial assessment of a report or any investigation.
  10. sanction: a temporary administrative restriction placed on a student’s enrolment that prevents a specific action by the student in relation to their course.
  11. Serious Academic Misconduct ([Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36), Section 3, a-c): includes academic misconduct which: 
    1. is, or appears from the available evidence to be, accompanied by a clear or demonstrable intention to flout or contravene the University’s requirements for academic honesty (including those set out in the Statute ([Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36)) and the AIP (Academic Integrity Policy and Procedure [Student Academic Misconduct Policy]), the GRP (Graduate Research Policy and Procedures) or any other policy or procedure regarding academic misconduct); 
    2. is, or appears from the available evidence to be, carefully and deliberately planned, repetitive, organised or systematic in nature; and
    3. is, or appears from the available evidence to be, significant in scale or scope.
  12. student: a person who was an enrolled student at a time when (they are) alleged to have engaged in academic misconduct (definition from [Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36))
  13. supervised assessment: an evaluation of student learning where students complete tasks under direct supervision. These assessments are used for measuring learning outcomes that assure CILOs, via mapped SILOs/MILOs in designated subjects. They are designed to ensure integrity through the following measures: 
    1. tasks are conducted in a controlled setting that incorporates direct observation;
    2. the identity of students is verified;
    3. access to external resources and unapproved technology and materials is restricted; and
    4. the use of AI is not permitted, except where AI use is being directly assessed.
  14. suspension: the temporary prohibition of a student from participating in University activities and accessing University facilities and services. A temporary prohibition may be for a specific period or until a condition or conditions have been met. A student’s rights will be restored, including the ability to re-enrol in the original or equivalent course or subject, at the conclusion of the suspension.
  15. unsupervised assessment: an evaluation of student learning where students complete tasks individually or in a group. These assessments support self-directed learning typically: 
    1. in an uncontrolled setting; and
    2. with access to resources chosen by students.

# Section 5 - Policy Statement
(3)  La Trobe University aspires to provide an outstanding student experience that is conducive to scholarly activity and supportive of individual learning goals. Underpinning this experience is a safe, inclusive, and respectful environment.
(4)  The University expects each person to be treated respectfully. Our behaviour must therefore afford dignity, courtesy, equality, and mutual respect, which we share across cultures, religions, and philosophies.
(5)  While studying at the University, students are entitled to:
  1. an environment free from unacceptable behaviour, including unlawful discrimination, harassment, sexual harm, bullying and hazing, violence or intimidation/threats of violence, vilification or victimisation;
  2. the right to exercise academic freedom and freedom of speech in accordance with the [Protection of Freedom of Speech and Academic Freedom Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=374) and the [Student Charter](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=225);
  3. raise issues, make enquiries or submit complaints in a reasonable and respectful manner and without being victimised; and
  4. merit-based decisions that afford procedural fairness.


### La Trobe’s Commitment to Students
(6)  La Trobe is committed to:
  1. providing and promoting an environment that is free from unacceptable behaviour that adversely impacts on the wellbeing of other members of the University community;
  2. providing an environment that promotes academic freedom and freedom of speech in accordance with the [Protection of Freedom of Speech and Academic Freedom Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=374) and the [Student Charter](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=225);
  3. taking all reasonable steps to ensure everyone is treated in accordance with our values and our policies/procedures;
  4. providing a complaints process to allow an opportunity to resolve behavioural issues in a timely manner, in accordance with procedural fairness and with information only shared on a need to know basis. See the [Student Complaints Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160) for more information about the University’s student complaint process;
  5. managing alleged sexual harm (which includes sexual harassment and assault) in accordance with the [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337) ;
  6. providing training and education to promote a respectful and inclusive culture at La Trobe University; and
  7. complying with the law.


### La Trobe’s Expectations of Students
(7)  La Trobe University expects students to treat everyone in accordance with La Trobe University’s values, policies, the [Student Charter](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=225) and the law.
(8)  Students must not, whether in person or online, engage in:
  1. unacceptable behaviour such as discrimination, harassment, sexual harm, bullying/hazing, violence, vilification and victimisation. Unacceptable behaviour includes behaviour which constitutes or may reasonably be perceived as: 
    1. an attack or threat to attack a person (physically, psychologically or sexually)
    2. verbal abuse or using offensive language
    3. intimidation
    4. causing injury
    5. the harassment of an individual or group.
  2. behaviour which: 
    1. breaches any of the provisions in the [Campus Access, Premises and Facilities Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=434);
    2. places the health, safety or reputation of anyone at risk;
    3. adversely impacts on the wellbeing of staff or students; or
    4. causes damage to or is likely to cause damage to La Trobe University property;
    5. may constitute general misconduct as defined in the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37); or
    6. is otherwise against the law (e.g. the purchase, consumption, selling, distribution or other engagement with illegal drugs on campus or in any La Trobe work or study environment.


### Alcohol and Drugs
(9)  Students are expected to demonstrate an understanding that as individuals they are responsible for their own behaviour, have an obligation to act responsibly and not be impaired by alcohol or drugs. The University will not tolerate unsafe, unwelcome or offensive behaviour caused by the irresponsible consumption of alcohol or drugs by students.
(10)  In order to protect the health and safety of themselves and other members of the University community, students must not:
  1. attend campus or present for any work or study (including online) impaired by alcohol or drugs, including prescription or over the counter medication;
  2. become impaired by the use of any substance while on campus or in any work or study environment (including online);
  3. consume, purchase, manufacture, sell, distribute or otherwise engage with illegal drugs on campus or in any La Trobe work or study environment;
  4. if taking prescription or over the counter medication that may have an impairing effect, students should discuss any adjustments that may be needed to your work or study with AccessAbility or teaching staff to ensure everyone's safety.


### Engagement in University Processes and Training
(11)  Students are expected to:
  1. complete the compulsory Respectful Behaviour and Culture module as part of their course requirements;
  2. participate in internal complaint, preliminary inquiry or investigation processes, where required. Such processes will be conducted by authorised areas of the University (e.g. Student Conduct and Complaints);
  3. contact Safer Community when they believe they have witnessed/experienced unacceptable behaviour in accordance with the relevant procedure;
  4. comply with the processes established by the relevant supporting procedures, including producing their student ID card or other form of photo identification when requested to do so by an authorised officer of the University; and
  5. understand that their student identification card is not transferable. The student ID card can only be used by the person named on the card and cannot be loaned or shared with another person.


### Consequences of a Breach
(12)  A breach of this Policy may result in disciplinary action in accordance with the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37), referral to other University processes or, in serious cases, referral to other agencies.

  2. [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337)

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=60#document-top)
# Section 7 - Definitions
(14)  For the purposes of this policy and procedure:
  1. bullying is the repeated, unreasonable and less favourable treatment of a person. It includes behaviour that intimidates, offends, degrades or humiliates a person and creates a risk to health and safety. Bullying can: 
    1. take many forms, including jokes, teasing, nicknames, emails, pictures, text messages, social isolation or ignoring people, or unfair work practices;
    2. involve many different forms of unreasonable behaviour, which can be obvious (direct) or subtle (indirect);
    3. be intentional, where someone’s actions are intended to humiliate, offend, intimidate or distress, whether or not the behaviour resulted in that effect; and
    4. be unintentional through engaging in behaviour that results in humiliation, offence, intimidation, distress and could reasonably have been expected to cause that effect.
  2. discrimination is when distinctions are made between individuals/groups so as to disadvantage some and advantage others. It can be classified as either direct or indirect: 
    1. direct Discrimination – when someone is treated less favourably than another person/group in a similar situation because of personal characteristics protected by law; and
    2. indirect Discrimination – when an unreasonable requirement, condition or practice is imposed that has, or is likely to have, the effect of disadvantaging people with a personal characteristic protected by law.
  3. harassment is when uninvited or unwelcome behaviour causes someone, or a group of people, to reasonably feel intimidated, insulted or humiliated. It can occur in a single incident or a series of incidents. Harassment may also be experienced as a result of witnessing behaviour not directed to that person e.g. overhearing an unacceptable joke. Each person perceives things differently as their values and experiences are unique to them. As such, they may react differently to how someone might expect.
  4. hazing is when students are not permitted to engage in any action taken or any situation created intentionally that causes embarrassment, harassment or ridicule and risks emotional and/or physical harm to an individual or members of a group or team, regardless of the person’s willingness to participate (often referred to as ‘hazing’). The difference between hazing and bullying is subtle, which is why they are often used interchangeably. The same power dynamics are involved, and the same intimidation tactics used. The only real difference between hazing and bullying is that bullying usually involves singling out an individual at any time and bullying them as a means to exclude them. Hazing, on the other hand, involves including people by having them ‘earn’ their way into a group or onto a team.
  5. sexual harassment refers to an unwelcome sexual advance, an unwelcome request for sexual favours or other unwelcome conduct of a sexual nature in person or via electronic/social media. It includes: 
    1. verbal forms such as making comments about someone’s appearance in a sexually suggestive way, unwelcome enquiries regarding a person’s sex life, requests for sex or repeated unwelcome requests for dates, telephone calls with a sexual undertone, continuous rude or sexist jokes/remarks, sexual insults or taunts, spreading sexual rumours, threats or non-consensual disclosure of a person’s sexual orientation, rating peers or colleagues with respect to sexual performance, sending sexually explicit emails or text messages;
    2. non-verbal forms such as gestures with a sexual meaning, staring at someone or making obscene gestures or noises, stalking (including cyber stalking), “flashing” or exposing body parts; and
    3. visual forms such as displaying objects or promotional material, reading materials, or other materials that are sexually demeaning or pornographic in nature.
  6. sexual harm: means misconduct of a sexual nature and includes: 
    1. sexual assault and rape;
    2. sexual harassment;
    3. sexual exploitation;
    4. Sexual abuse;
    5. any conduct of a sexual nature without consent, including: 
      1. obscene, indecent, threatening language or behaviour (including indecent exposure);
      2. observation, filming or distributing an image of a person’s genital or anal region or an intimate image without consent (eg revenge pornography);
      3. drink spiking;
      4. stalking; or
      5. hazing of a sexual nature.

sections.text:
(1)  La Trobe Universty’s Student Charter outlines the rights and responsibilities of students while enrolled at La Trobe University.
(2)  This Student Charter embodies the core values that we hold as a community and the partnership that exists between all students, short course participants, and the University.
(3)  The Student Charter is published in accordance with the University’s obligations under the [Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards) 2021](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?standard=4), the [Education Services for Overseas Students (ESOS) Act](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=57), the [Higher Education Support Act 2003](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=78) and the [Higher Education Provider Amendment (Support for Students Policy) Guidelines 2023](https://www.legislation.gov.au/Details/F2023L01679).

sections.heading: Section 2 - Purpose
sections.text:
(1)  This Policy outlines La Trobe University’s expectations regarding communication between the University and students to ensure such communication occurs responsibly, effectively and in compliance with relevant laws and Standards, including but not limited to:
  1. the [Spam Act 2003 (Cth)](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=56)
  2. the [Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards) 2021](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?standard=4)
  3. the [National Code of Practice for Registration Authorities and Providers of Higher Education and Training to Overseas Students](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?code=2) (ESOS National Code)
  4. the [Disability Discrimination Act 1992](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=47), and relevant accessibility instruments and guidelines including [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/)

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)

Section 4 - Key Decisions

sections.heading: Section 5 - Policy Statement
Part A - Accessibility
Part B - Official Communications with Students
sections.text:
(13)  The University’s channels for official correspondence with students are students’ La Trobe email accounts and text messages. Communication through text messages is reserved for communications that are considered important, time-sensitive, or require students to take action on a particular matter. Other communication methods with students include StudentOnLine, web pages, FAQs, Chatbot, the Learning Management System (LMS), campus digital signage, posters, flyers, newsletters and social media.
(14)  Students are responsible for checking their La Trobe email regularly and for monitoring their phone for text messages. The University is not responsible for delivery failures due to user or system negligence.
(15)  The University deems official correspondence sent by email and text message to have been delivered when the correspondence has been sent to the official La Trobe email account or personal mobile number, and where University systems have not recorded a genuine bounced message or undelivered notice.

sections.heading: Approval for Broadcast Communications with Students
sections.text:
(16)  Broadcast emails and text messages may be sent to students only where they have been approved by the relevant approval authority or their nominee. The following roles are authorised to approve broadcast messages to large student groups (e.g. all enrolled students, students enrolled at a particular campus, students enrolled in a particular School and other cohorts such as all international students and all graduate researchers):
  1. the Vice-Chancellor and any member of the University’s Senior Executive Group
  2. Pro Vice-Chancellors or nominee(s)
  3. any Head of Division, Director or nominee(s)
  4. Deans or nominee(s)
  5. the Senior Manager, Student Communications or nominee(s)
  6. Incident Commander(s) and Incident Communications representative (Director, Media and Communications)


(17)  All other staff members of the University can discuss proposals to send a broadcast email or text message by consulting the Student Communications team.
(18)  The Student Communications team is responsible for ensuring broadcast communications under its remit meet branding and editorial guidelines and align with relevant University policies (e.g. those outlined in Section 5 of this Policy).

sections.heading: Student Use of Communication Channels
sections.text:
(19)  In accordance with the [IS Acceptable Use Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=418), when seeking advice about student matters from staff or divisions of the University, coursework students must use their La Trobe student email account. Where graduate research students have an institutional staff account this may be used when corresponding with their supervisors or staff within their school; however they must use their student email account for all official correspondence related to their course.
(20)  Students are not permitted to send broadcast emails or use other University email lists without relevant approvals (as outlined above). While students may send appropriate emails to other students in their subject/s or course, unsolicited emailing or SPAM is strictly prohibited. Students must also ensure that they use social media in accordance with relevant University policies (see the [Student Charter](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=225), the [Student Behaviours Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=60), the [IS Acceptable Use Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=418), the [SPAM Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=68) and [advice on the use of social media](https://www.latrobe.edu.au/students/admin/rights-and-responsibilities/your-responsibilities/general-conduct/social-media)).
(21)  Students within the scope of this Policy may not opt out of correspondence via their official La Trobe student email account but may opt out of:
  1. promotional or marketing emails;
  2. forum digest communications on the LMS.

sections.heading: Part C - Other Communications with Students
sections.text:
(22)  Staff responsible for other communication channels such as university websites, campus digital signage, posters, flyers, newsletters, and social media must comply with the principles outlined in this Policy and seek approval for the content and design of the communication from their immediate supervisor.
(23)  The following communications do not require authorisation:
  1. one-to-one enquiries or transactional communications between students and any staff member of the University;
  2. course-related (curricular) communications between students and teaching staff.

sections.heading: Part D - Recordkeeping
sections.text: (24)  Records of student communications must be retained in accordance with the University’s Records Management Policy and relevant Public Records Office of Victoria Retention and Disposal Authority provisions (see [Quick Reference Guides on the LTU intranet](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/tasks-and-processes/records-and-archiving/retention-and-disposal#accordion-397495-5)). In accordance with the Student Support Retention and Disposal Authority records of communications that constitute broad advice to students do not need to be retained beyond their period of relevance.

sections.heading: Part E - Review
sections.text:
(25)  Students who are still dissatisfied with the application of any part of this Policy may lodge a complaint under the provisions of the [Student Complaints Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160).
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)

sections.heading: Section 7 - Definitions
sections.text:
(26)  For the purposes of this Policy:
  1. Official University Correspondence: correspondence created or received by a staff member or contractor of the University in the conduct of University business relating to the obligations or entitlements of students. This may include one-to-one communications and the following: 
    1. automated communications: authorised emails and text messages which are sent to students, including those that are triggered automatically via student systems/platforms;
    2. broadcast communications: authorised messages distributed/posted simultaneously to a large cohort or the entire student body using any broad-based channel (including email and text message). These communications can be personalised or non-personalised and serve various purposes including but not limited to administrative, informational/support, promotional or emergency.
  2. Spam: irrelevant or unsolicited digital messaging sent to a large number of students.
  3. student email account: the account issued automatically to every student through which they may send and receive official university correspondence.
  4. student: defined in the La Trobe University Act 2009 as: 
    1. a person enrolled at the University in a course leading to a degree or other award; 
    2. a person who is designated as a student or is of a class of persons designated as students by the Council. 
  5. student cohort: a group of students that have shared characteristics such as (but not limited to) campus, school or course of enrolment, student type (domestic or international) or fee status.
  6. university email system: central messaging systems hosted by Information Services to provide messaging and collaboration services, including email to students of the University.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)

sections.text:
(27)  This Policy is made under the [La Trobe University Act 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=8).
(28)  Associated information includes:
  1. [Brand language and editorial style guides](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/support-services-and-divisions/future-growth/marketing,-digital-and-insights/creative-and-production/about-digital-creative/publications/brand-language-editorial-style-guide) (staff only)
  2. [Student Communications intranet page](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/learning-and-teaching/student-support-and-engagement/student-communications) (staff only)
  3. [Student Communications request form](https://latrobeuni.sharepoint.com/sites/applications/sc/) (staff only)
  4. [Universal Design and Inclusion Action Plan](https://www.latrobe.edu.au/about/at-a-glance/plans/documents/LTU-Universal-Design-Inclusion-Action-Plan.pdf)

# Section 2 - Purpose
(1)  This Policy outlines La Trobe University’s expectations regarding communication between the University and students to ensure such communication occurs responsibly, effectively and in compliance with relevant laws and Standards, including but not limited to:
  1. the [Spam Act 2003 (Cth)](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=56)
  2. the [Higher Education Standards Framework (Threshold Standards) 2021](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?standard=4)
  3. the [National Code of Practice for Registration Authorities and Providers of Higher Education and Training to Overseas Students](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?code=2) (ESOS National Code)
  4. the [Disability Discrimination Act 1992](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=47), and relevant accessibility instruments and guidelines including [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG21/)

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)
# Section 3 - Scope
(2)  This Policy applies to:
  1. current students, being students who: 
    1. have accepted an offer, been admitted to and/or who are enrolled in a course of the University (including in enabling and short courses);
    2. are on an approved Leave of Absence or currently suspended from their course;
    3. are absent from their course (up to the point where they receive a notification that their status is to be recorded as Absent Without Official Leave [AWOL]);
    4. have completed course requirements but have outstanding matters (e.g. refunds, graduation);
    5. are graduate research students under examination, or whose candidature has lapsed.
  2. all communications with current students, including: 
    1. communications related to student administration, academic progress, student services, events, University operations, safety and critical incidents and any other issues related to the student experience;
    2. one-to-one enquiries or transactional communications between students and any staff member of the University;
    3. course-related (curricular) communications between students and teaching staff.


(3)  This Policy applies to communications with students enrolled in La Trobe courses through third-party teaching partners. Local arrangements apply for ensuring accessibility and authorisation of broadcast communications originating from the partner organisation.
(4)  This Policy does not apply to communication with graduates (alumni), past students, potential students (including applicants for admission).
(5)  This Policy does not restrict:
  1. broadcast emails from the Vice-Chancellor (or nominee);
  2. emergency announcements or alerts, on matters concerning: 
    1. critical incidents, local and global emergencies
    2. potential health, safety or wellbeing issues
    3. IT and building facility outages and service upgrades
  3. correspondence for a mainly commercial or promotional purpose.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)
# Section 4 - Key Decisions  
| Key Decisions/Responsibilities  | Role  |  
| --- | --- |  
| Authorise broadcast emails to students of the University  | Positions specified in Part B  |  
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)
# Section 5 - Policy Statement
(6)  The University aims to ensure:
  1. student communication enhances the student experience and engagement, and supports the University’s strategic goals and objectives;
  2. students receive timely, accurate and meaningful information, delivered through the most appropriate channel.


(7)  All communications with students are subject to the University’s other relevant policies, including but not limited to:
  1. the [Disability Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=284)
  2. the [Enrolment Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=393)
  3. the [Information Security Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=69)
  4. the [IS Acceptable Use Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=418)
  5. the [Privacy Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=1)
  6. the [Records Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=10)
  7. the [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337)
  8. the [SPAM Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=68)
  9. the [Student Charter](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=225)
  10. the [Student Support Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=409).


(8)  All student communications must be:
  1. accessible: able to be accessed by students with diverse needs, or be adapted on request;
  2. inclusive: designed in accordance with inclusive design principles to ensure equitable access for students with disabilities, neurodiverse learners, students from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds and student with diverse identities, including gender identity;
  3. culturally safe and respectful: recognising that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students may have distinct cultural contexts and ensuring these are considered in the design and delivery of student communications, particularly where communications relate to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander matters;
  4. student-centric: focused on student needs, informed by student priorities and co-designed with students where possible and practical;
  5. audience-specific: targeted, tailored and (when possible) personalised;
  6. accurate and timely: correct, reliable up to date and aligned to the student lifecycle;
  7. respectful: polite, courteous, professional and helpful;
  8. in clear, everyday English: easily understood by a diverse audience;
  9. actionable: action-orientated with clear instructions and links to more detailed information;
  10. lawful: all official communications comply with relevant legislation and policies.


(9)  Any broadcast communications must, in addition to the above, align with University branding and editorial guides (see Section 8).
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)
# Section 6 - Procedures
## Part A - Accessibility
(10)  The Student Communications team reviews templates, content and communications under its remit to maximise accessibility through the use of clear everyday English and other accessibility and inclusivity principles outlined in this Policy.
(11)  Students who require any additional support to access student communications can contact the [Accessibility Hub](https://www.latrobe.edu.au/students/support/wellbeing/services/accessibility-hub) to arrange for a Learning Access Plan (LAP). LAPs enable students to access appropriate inclusive resources via the Library and other areas of the University.
(12)  The Senior Manager, Student Communications is responsible for:
  1. supporting accessibility audits of student-facing communication platforms and content to ensure compliance with the University’s [Website and Intranet Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=32);
  2. arranging surveys and other feedback mechanisms on the accessibility and effectiveness of the University’s communications with students;
  3. documenting audit outcomes and ensuring that any recommendations for improvement are implemented in responsible areas;
  4. consulting with teams including but not limited to Accessibility, Prevention and Inclusion and Digital Services to address identified gaps and ensure inclusive design principles are upheld across all communication channels.


## Part B - Official Communications with Students
(13)  The University’s channels for official correspondence with students are students’ La Trobe email accounts and text messages. Communication through text messages is reserved for communications that are considered important, time-sensitive, or require students to take action on a particular matter. Other communication methods with students include StudentOnLine, web pages, FAQs, Chatbot, the Learning Management System (LMS), campus digital signage, posters, flyers, newsletters and social media.
(14)  Students are responsible for checking their La Trobe email regularly and for monitoring their phone for text messages. The University is not responsible for delivery failures due to user or system negligence.
(15)  The University deems official correspondence sent by email and text message to have been delivered when the correspondence has been sent to the official La Trobe email account or personal mobile number, and where University systems have not recorded a genuine bounced message or undelivered notice.
### Approval for Broadcast Communications with Students
(16)  Broadcast emails and text messages may be sent to students only where they have been approved by the relevant approval authority or their nominee. The following roles are authorised to approve broadcast messages to large student groups (e.g. all enrolled students, students enrolled at a particular campus, students enrolled in a particular School and other cohorts such as all international students and all graduate researchers):
  1. the Vice-Chancellor and any member of the University’s Senior Executive Group
  2. Pro Vice-Chancellors or nominee(s)
  3. any Head of Division, Director or nominee(s)
  4. Deans or nominee(s)
  5. the Senior Manager, Student Communications or nominee(s)
  6. Incident Commander(s) and Incident Communications representative (Director, Media and Communications)


(17)  All other staff members of the University can discuss proposals to send a broadcast email or text message by consulting the Student Communications team.
(18)  The Student Communications team is responsible for ensuring broadcast communications under its remit meet branding and editorial guidelines and align with relevant University policies (e.g. those outlined in Section 5 of this Policy).
### Student Use of Communication Channels
(19)  In accordance with the [IS Acceptable Use Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=418), when seeking advice about student matters from staff or divisions of the University, coursework students must use their La Trobe student email account. Where graduate research students have an institutional staff account this may be used when corresponding with their supervisors or staff within their school; however they must use their student email account for all official correspondence related to their course.
(20)  Students are not permitted to send broadcast emails or use other University email lists without relevant approvals (as outlined above). While students may send appropriate emails to other students in their subject/s or course, unsolicited emailing or SPAM is strictly prohibited. Students must also ensure that they use social media in accordance with relevant University policies (see the [Student Charter](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=225), the [Student Behaviours Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=60), the [IS Acceptable Use Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=418), the [SPAM Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=68) and [advice on the use of social media](https://www.latrobe.edu.au/students/admin/rights-and-responsibilities/your-responsibilities/general-conduct/social-media)).
(21)  Students within the scope of this Policy may not opt out of correspondence via their official La Trobe student email account but may opt out of:
  1. promotional or marketing emails;
  2. forum digest communications on the LMS.


## Part C - Other Communications with Students
(22)  Staff responsible for other communication channels such as university websites, campus digital signage, posters, flyers, newsletters, and social media must comply with the principles outlined in this Policy and seek approval for the content and design of the communication from their immediate supervisor.
(23)  The following communications do not require authorisation:
  1. one-to-one enquiries or transactional communications between students and any staff member of the University;
  2. course-related (curricular) communications between students and teaching staff.


## Part D - Recordkeeping
(24)  Records of student communications must be retained in accordance with the University’s Records Management Policy and relevant Public Records Office of Victoria Retention and Disposal Authority provisions (see [Quick Reference Guides on the LTU intranet](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/tasks-and-processes/records-and-archiving/retention-and-disposal#accordion-397495-5)). In accordance with the Student Support Retention and Disposal Authority records of communications that constitute broad advice to students do not need to be retained beyond their period of relevance.
## Part E - Review
(25)  Students who are still dissatisfied with the application of any part of this Policy may lodge a complaint under the provisions of the [Student Complaints Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160).
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)
# Section 7 - Definitions
(26)  For the purposes of this Policy:
  1. Official University Correspondence: correspondence created or received by a staff member or contractor of the University in the conduct of University business relating to the obligations or entitlements of students. This may include one-to-one communications and the following: 
    1. automated communications: authorised emails and text messages which are sent to students, including those that are triggered automatically via student systems/platforms;
    2. broadcast communications: authorised messages distributed/posted simultaneously to a large cohort or the entire student body using any broad-based channel (including email and text message). These communications can be personalised or non-personalised and serve various purposes including but not limited to administrative, informational/support, promotional or emergency.
  2. Spam: irrelevant or unsolicited digital messaging sent to a large number of students.
  3. student email account: the account issued automatically to every student through which they may send and receive official university correspondence.
  4. student: defined in the La Trobe University Act 2009 as: 
    1. a person enrolled at the University in a course leading to a degree or other award; 
    2. a person who is designated as a student or is of a class of persons designated as students by the Council. 
  5. student cohort: a group of students that have shared characteristics such as (but not limited to) campus, school or course of enrolment, student type (domestic or international) or fee status.
  6. university email system: central messaging systems hosted by Information Services to provide messaging and collaboration services, including email to students of the University.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=212#document-top)
# Section 8 - Authority and Associated Information
(27)  This Policy is made under the [La Trobe University Act 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=8).
(28)  Associated information includes:
  1. [Brand language and editorial style guides](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/support-services-and-divisions/future-growth/marketing,-digital-and-insights/creative-and-production/about-digital-creative/publications/brand-language-editorial-style-guide) (staff only)
  2. [Student Communications intranet page](https://intranet.latrobe.edu.au/learning-and-teaching/student-support-and-engagement/student-communications) (staff only)
  3. [Student Communications request form](https://latrobeuni.sharepoint.com/sites/applications/sc/) (staff only)
  4. [Universal Design and Inclusion Action Plan](https://www.latrobe.edu.au/about/at-a-glance/plans/documents/LTU-Universal-Design-Inclusion-Action-Plan.pdf)

sections.heading: Section 2 - Purpose
Section 3 - Scope
sections.text:
(2)  Unless specifically exempted in this document, this Policy applies to the following individuals (for ease of reference all are referred to as students, or where appropriate, complainants in this policy):
  1. persons seeking admission to, or currently or previously enrolled in, any La Trobe University subject or award course, including those conducted by third parties; and
  2. participants in short courses.


(3)  Complaints should be lodged within 12 months of the issue or incident. The University may consider complaints submitted after this period where it determines that there are exceptional circumstances that include the student’s ability to engage with the complaints process.
(4)  The student complaints process may be used to submit complaints about:
  1. service delivery/administration issues, including university facilities;
  2. matters of process related to the University experience;
  3. academic standards and educational quality issues;
  4. third parties while providing services on behalf of the University, such as contractors, education agents and third party providers, including those individuals and organisations supervising student placements and student accommodation.


(5)  Complaints may be informal (resolution is sought at the local level) or formal (lodged through the Student Complaints Management System) and are distinguished from:
  1. enquiries directed to the University by individuals; or 
  2. feedback given through other channels without expectation of a response.


(6)  The student complaints process does not include complaints about inappropriate conduct or behaviour by students, staff or third parties. All conduct and behaviour complaints received by the Student Complaints service are directly referred to Safer Community within the Integrity Office and are managed in accordance with the [Student Conduct Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382) or the [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337), or other relevant policy as appropriate.
(7)  Where a student wishes to seek a review of, or lodge an appeal against, specific decisions of the University they may be referred to other relevant statutes, policies or procedures. For student matters, this includes but is not limited to disputes regarding:
  1. eligibility for Special Consideration (refer to the [Assessment Procedure – Adjustments [incorporating Special Consideration]](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=380));
  2. academic progress determinations ([Academic Progress Statute 2010](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=82) and associated policies);
  3. academic misconduct determinations ([Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36), [Student Academic Misconduct Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=221)).

sections.text:
(8)  Consumers of any La Trobe University services who are not La Trobe students, including students of other institutions who reside in La Trobe University student accommodation, may submit a complaint through the Student Complaints Office. The Student Complaints Office may facilitate a response by engaging with the relevant area of the University.
