sections.heading: Section 5 - Policy Statement
Section 6 - Procedures
sections.text:
(14)  The University has an established Student Complaints Office and a [Student Complaints Management System (SCM)](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=60&version=4&associated) to coordinate the management of complaints at no cost to complainants.
(15)  All parties to a complaint are entitled to bring a support person to meetings and discussions, should a meeting or discussion be required. A support person can be any person chosen by the party. The support person’s role is to observe the meeting and provide support and guidance, as requested, but they may not speak on behalf of the party they are supporting. This does not exclude the presence of a translator, Auslan interpreter or other interpreter or person to enable equitable and meaningful participation by international students, Deaf/deaf, disabled or neurodivergent parties.

sections.heading: Part A - Complaints Pathways
sections.text:
(16)  Individuals may choose to pursue a complaint through two (2) key pathways:
  1. complainants are encouraged to attempt to resolve matters informally at the local level, where it is reasonable and appropriate to do so; or
  2. where individuals are not comfortable engaging in local level resolution, or if an attempt at local level resolution has been unsuccessful, they may submit a formal complaint following the process outlined in Part C of this Procedure.


(17)  Confidential, independent and free Student Advocacy Services are provided to assist current students to speak to staff members about their concerns. Information about other support services available to students and to participants enrolled in short courses is provided on the [Student Complaints webpage](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=60&version=4&associated).

sections.heading: Part B - Local Level Resolution
sections.text:
(18)  A local level resolution may involve the student discussing the matter directly with the person with whom they have the grievance, or with a staff member in the school or relevant business area.
(19)  Students are encouraged to identify causes and desired outcomes for the complaint issue before speaking either directly to the person concerned, or to the staff member with whom they are lodging their complaint. Students may wish to do this in conjunction with a support service, such as Student Advocacy.
(20)  When a staff member becomes aware of a student issue they should, where appropriate, endeavour to resolve the issue to the satisfaction of all parties. All solutions offered and implemented must be in accordance with La Trobe policies.
(21)  In the process of resolving the complaint the staff member may:
  1. refer the issue to a senior staff member from within the relevant school/business area for advice; or
  2. direct the student to appropriate support services where required.

sections.heading: Part C - Submitting a Formal Complaint
Part D - Complaint Investigation
Possible Outcomes
Determination and Implementation of Outcomes
sections.text:
(34)  The relevant school or business area must make a determination regarding the proposed outcome and provide a response to the Student Complaints Office within 10 business days of the complaint being referred to the area.
(35)  Where the responsible person within the Student Complaints Office has any concerns regarding the appropriateness of the proposed outcome they will escalate the matter to the Director, Integrity Office.
(36)  Where a complaint outcome results in a decision or recommendation in favour of the complainant, the relevant school or business area must immediately implement the decision or recommendation and/or take the preventative or corrective action required.

sections.heading: Communication of Outcomes to Students
Part F - Review of Complaint Outcomes
sections.text:
(39)  Complainants who are dissatisfied with any aspect of how this Policy has been applied, or the outcome of their complaint, may seek a review through the Office of the University Ombudsman, under the provisions of the La Trobe University [Ombudsman Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=62). 
(40)  Complainants may also choose to lodge a complaint with an external organisation such as the Australian Human Rights Commission, the Victorian Privacy Commissioner, Victoria Police or the [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated). Some external agencies require that all relevant University complaints processes have been exhausted before they will consider the matter. For further information on complaints considered by the [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated), go to [Making a complaint | National Student Ombudsman (NSO)](https://www.nso.gov.au/making-a-complaint).
(41)  If a complaint is accepted for investigation by an external organisation, the University will normally suspend any in-progress review or University investigation until the external investigation has been completed and all reports submitted.
(42)  The Student Complaints Office may assist complainants to determine whether another organisation can handle the matter more effectively.

sections.heading: Part G - Withdrawing a Complaint
sections.text:
(43)  A complainant may withdraw a complaint at any time by advising the Student Complaints Office.
(44)  In cases where a complaint has been withdrawn the University retains the right to investigate and address matters raised in that complaint in order to meet its obligations to all students, participants and staff to maintain, as far as is reasonably practicable, a safe and healthy work and study environment. In such instances the confidentiality of the original complainant will be preserved unless this conflicts with the University’s duty of care obligations, or obligations required by law.
(45)  The University makes no undertaking to expunge any records of withdrawn complaints.

sections.heading: Part H - Recording and Reporting of Complaints
Section 7 - Definitions
sections.text:
(53)  For the purposes of this Policy and Procedure:
  1. anonymous complaints: where the person making the complaint withholds their name or identity.
  2. complaint: an implied or express statement of dissatisfaction where a response is sought, reasonable to expect, or legally required. Complaints are considered: 
    1. informal, where a student or individual seeks a resolution at the local level;
    2. formal, where a student or individual lodges a complaint through the University’s Student Complaints Management system.
  3. complainant: a person who has made a complaint about an aspect of the University or the University environment.
  4. conflict of interest: interest, involvement or information which may influence or be perceived to influence a person’s ability to make objective recommendations or decisions in investigating a complaint.
  5. exceptional circumstances: those circumstances that are beyond an individual’s control for which there was no opportunity to prepare in advance.
  6. external agencies: agencies outside the University, for example, the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission, Australian Human Rights Commission, Independent Broad Based Anti-Corruption Commission, [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated) or Victoria Police.
  7. partially substantiated complaint: part of the substance of the complaint is established based on the available evidence, and part is unsubstantiated.
  8. participant: a person registered in a short course run by the University.
  9. Procedural Fairness: a legal concept that is sometimes used interchangeably with natural justice. What is procedurally fair will depend on the circumstances but generally involves: 
    1. the right to be told of allegations in sufficient detail to enable a person to respond. This will not necessarily involve the person being given all information, and some confidential information and original documents may not necessarily be provided;
    2. an opportunity to answer to allegations before any decision is made, including sufficient time to respond;
    3. a requirement that a decision maker is not biased and gives genuine consideration to whatever response is given by a person.
  10. parties to the complaint: University staff members or students who are the subject of a complaint.
  11. staff of the University: academic staff including contract staff, visiting appointments, conjoint appointments and guest lecturers; professional and technical staff (including casual and contract staff); staff of partner institutions teaching La Trobe courses.
  12. substantiated complaint: the substance of the complaint is established based on the available evidence.
  13. university community: all students, staff, visitors to the University, contractors and other workers employed by the University, University tenants and their staff.
  14. unsubstantiated complaint: the substance of the complaint is unable to be established based on the available evidence, or the available evidence disproves the substance of the complaint.
  15. vexatious: where a complaint is made in bad faith to cause harm to an individual.
  16. victimisation: subjecting or threatening to subject another person to any detriment because that person, in good faith, has made a complaint, or supported someone in making a complaint or raising a grievance, or provided information during an investigation of a complaint or grievance.

# Section 1 - Key Information  
| Policy Type and Approval Body  | Administrative – Vice-Chancellor  |  
| --- | --- |  
| Accountable Executive – Policy  | Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic)  |  
| Responsible Manager – Policy  | Director, Integrity Office  |  
| Review Date  | 11 June 2029  |  
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160#document-top)
# Section 2 - Purpose
(1)  This Policy outlines the mechanisms for students (and other relevant individuals outlined in the Scope section) to lodge a complaint about an aspect of University life including academic and non-academic matters. The Policy aligns with the following key legislation and codes:
  1. the [Higher Education Standards Framework 2021](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?standard=4) (HESF);
  2. the [Educational Services for Overseas Students Act 2000 (Cth)](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=57) and the [National Code of Practice for Providers of Education and Training to Overseas Students 2018](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=402&version=1&associated) - Standard 10;
  3. [Statement of Regulatory Expectations: Student grievance and complaint mechanisms](https://www.teqsa.gov.au/how-we-regulate/statements-regulatory-expectations/statement-regulatory-expectations-student-grievance-and-complaint-mechanisms).

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160#document-top)
# Section 3 - Scope
(2)  Unless specifically exempted in this document, this Policy applies to the following individuals (for ease of reference all are referred to as students, or where appropriate, complainants in this policy):
  1. persons seeking admission to, or currently or previously enrolled in, any La Trobe University subject or award course, including those conducted by third parties; and
  2. participants in short courses.


(3)  Complaints should be lodged within 12 months of the issue or incident. The University may consider complaints submitted after this period where it determines that there are exceptional circumstances that include the student’s ability to engage with the complaints process.
(4)  The student complaints process may be used to submit complaints about:
  1. service delivery/administration issues, including university facilities;
  2. matters of process related to the University experience;
  3. academic standards and educational quality issues;
  4. third parties while providing services on behalf of the University, such as contractors, education agents and third party providers, including those individuals and organisations supervising student placements and student accommodation.


(5)  Complaints may be informal (resolution is sought at the local level) or formal (lodged through the Student Complaints Management System) and are distinguished from:
  1. enquiries directed to the University by individuals; or 
  2. feedback given through other channels without expectation of a response.


(6)  The student complaints process does not include complaints about inappropriate conduct or behaviour by students, staff or third parties. All conduct and behaviour complaints received by the Student Complaints service are directly referred to Safer Community within the Integrity Office and are managed in accordance with the [Student Conduct Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382) or the [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337), or other relevant policy as appropriate.
(7)  Where a student wishes to seek a review of, or lodge an appeal against, specific decisions of the University they may be referred to other relevant statutes, policies or procedures. For student matters, this includes but is not limited to disputes regarding:
  1. eligibility for Special Consideration (refer to the [Assessment Procedure – Adjustments [incorporating Special Consideration]](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=380));
  2. academic progress determinations ([Academic Progress Statute 2010](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=82) and associated policies);
  3. academic misconduct determinations ([Academic Integrity Statute 2015](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=36), [Student Academic Misconduct Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=221)).


### Complaints from the Public and Non-La Trobe students
(8)  Consumers of any La Trobe University services who are not La Trobe students, including students of other institutions who reside in La Trobe University student accommodation, may submit a complaint through the Student Complaints Office. The Student Complaints Office may facilitate a response by engaging with the relevant area of the University.
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160#document-top)
# Section 4 - Key Decisions  
| Key Decisions  |  Role  |  
| --- | --- |  
| Appointment of an investigator  | Manager, Student Complaints and Appeals  |  
| Determination of complaint outcomes  | Director, Integrity Office or nominee  |  
| Communication of outcomes to student/s  | Manager, Student Complaints and Appeals  |  
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160#document-top)
# Section 5 - Policy Statement
(9)  As part of its commitment to quality, La Trobe University recognises the need for an effective complaints mechanism to adequately resolve student grievances and complaints about University life.
(10)  The University seeks to provide a student complaints service that:
  1. is free of charge, easily accessible for all students, and sensitive to the needs of the diverse community in which it operates;
  2. takes a person-centred and trauma-informed approach in the handling of sensitive complaints;
  3. safeguards student rights and wellbeing;
  4. identifies systemic issues at the University;
  5. supports quality improvement;
  6. investigates and resolves complaints in a timely manner;
  7. applies principles of Procedural Fairness, as appropriate;
  8. attempts to resolve complaints as close to the source as possible;
  9. does not pursue investigations of vexatious complaints or complaints without substance; and
  10. is free from victimisation and reprisal.


(11)  The complaints process complements other University processes where students may make enquiries, provide feedback, raise concerns or seek a review of or appeal against certain decisions of the University. The complaints process cannot be used as an alternative avenue for review or appeal processes that are established through other University statutes or policies.
(12)  The University expects students to make complaints in good faith. This means that complaints are made about a genuine concern, and not for the purpose of causing annoyance or malicious harm to another person.
(13)  Complaints will be managed in accordance with the University [Privacy Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=1). This means, among other things, that:
  1. complaints will be treated by all parties with appropriate confidentiality;
  2. each complaint resolution process is conducted by as few people as possible;
  3. complaint records may be disclosed to appropriate officers of the University or external authorities, as part of the University’s duty of care obligations, or as required by law;
  4. de-identified data may be used by the University for the purposes of reporting on the management of student complaints;
  5. information systems and records are maintained securely and confidentially as necessary to document and record responses to formal complaints.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160#document-top)
# Section 6 - Procedures
(14)  The University has an established Student Complaints Office and a [Student Complaints Management System (SCM)](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=60&version=4&associated) to coordinate the management of complaints at no cost to complainants.
(15)  All parties to a complaint are entitled to bring a support person to meetings and discussions, should a meeting or discussion be required. A support person can be any person chosen by the party. The support person’s role is to observe the meeting and provide support and guidance, as requested, but they may not speak on behalf of the party they are supporting. This does not exclude the presence of a translator, Auslan interpreter or other interpreter or person to enable equitable and meaningful participation by international students, Deaf/deaf, disabled or neurodivergent parties.
## Part A - Complaints Pathways
(16)  Individuals may choose to pursue a complaint through two (2) key pathways:
  1. complainants are encouraged to attempt to resolve matters informally at the local level, where it is reasonable and appropriate to do so; or
  2. where individuals are not comfortable engaging in local level resolution, or if an attempt at local level resolution has been unsuccessful, they may submit a formal complaint following the process outlined in Part C of this Procedure.


(17)  Confidential, independent and free Student Advocacy Services are provided to assist current students to speak to staff members about their concerns. Information about other support services available to students and to participants enrolled in short courses is provided on the [Student Complaints webpage](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=60&version=4&associated).
## Part B - Local Level Resolution
(18)  A local level resolution may involve the student discussing the matter directly with the person with whom they have the grievance, or with a staff member in the school or relevant business area.
(19)  Students are encouraged to identify causes and desired outcomes for the complaint issue before speaking either directly to the person concerned, or to the staff member with whom they are lodging their complaint. Students may wish to do this in conjunction with a support service, such as Student Advocacy.
(20)  When a staff member becomes aware of a student issue they should, where appropriate, endeavour to resolve the issue to the satisfaction of all parties. All solutions offered and implemented must be in accordance with La Trobe policies.
(21)  In the process of resolving the complaint the staff member may:
  1. refer the issue to a senior staff member from within the relevant school/business area for advice; or
  2. direct the student to appropriate support services where required.


## Part C - Submitting a Formal Complaint
(22)  In cases where direct and informal local level resolution is not appropriate or successful, or the student does not feel comfortable to pursue this path, the student may lodge a formal complaint in writing via the following channels:
  1. the online form provided on the [Student Complaints website](https://www.latrobe.edu.au/students/support/complaints) to formally register the complaint in the University’s SCM;
  2. email ([studentcomplaints@latrobe.edu.au](http://studentcomplaints@latrobe.edu.au)) or registered post to: La Trobe University, Melbourne, Victoria 3086 (ATT: Student Complaints Office).


(23)  Each complaint must specify the details of the matter about which the complaint is being made and the desired outcome. For the purposes of conducting an investigation and the provision of an outcome, contact details must normally be provided.
(24)  Where complainants elect to remain anonymous when lodging a complaint:
  1. this may restrict the University’s ability to assist, or may limit the complaint outcomes available to a student;
  2. the complaint may be accepted as feedback on the relevant issue or area and action taken where appropriate.


(25)  Complainants may request that their identity is withheld during an investigation. In these circumstances, only the staff member managing the complaint will know the identity of the complainant, subject to any disclosures required as outlined in Clause 13c above.
(26)  Complainants who require assistance or advice in preparing their complaint may seek assistance from a relevant support service, such as Student Advocacy.
(27)  The Student Complaints Office acknowledges the receipt and commences assessment of complaints submitted via the online form/SCM within 10 business days. The acknowledgment to complainants includes advice regarding:
  1. pathways to resolution of issues not formally considered complaints, for example, requests for information or review of decisions;
  2. actions to be undertaken in respect of the complaint;
  3. time frames in which it is expected that these processes will occur. Complainants will also be informed if the Student Complaints Office considers that their complaint may take longer than 60 calendar days to resolve, either at the commencement of the investigation process or during the course of the investigation;
  4. available support services.


## Part D - Complaint Investigation
(28)  When a complaint is lodged, the Student Complaints Office may contact the complainant to gather information about the circumstances of their complaint, to clarify their concerns and identify possible avenues for resolution.
(29)  The Student Complaints Office manages the complaint process, including:
  1. conducting an initial assessment of the complaint and appointing an investigator where appropriate;
  2. notifying the parties of the investigation and providing information regarding processes and timelines, including progress updates to complainants and respondents at agreed intervals;
  3. arranging investigation activities such as interviews;
  4. gathering any information required for the investigation, including relevant policies, procedures and protocols;
  5. handling final communications to all parties.


(30)  Where it is determined that investigation of a complaint is required the Manager, Student Complaints and Appeals appoints an investigator who may be:
  1. a staff member from within the Student Complaints Office; or
  2. a staff member from either within the relevant school or business area or another area of the University. The staff member responsible for investigating the complaint must not have a real or perceived conflict of interest, including any prior involvement in the complaint.


(31)  In serious or complex circumstances, a complaint may be referred to another area of the University, such as People & Culture and/or Legal Services. Where this occurs the Student Complaints Office continues to monitor the progress of the complaint and maintains records of the outcome.
(32)  Where appropriate the Student Complaints Office may recommend to the parties that mediation or other alternative dispute resolution methods may be suitable for resolving the matter.
## Part E - Outcomes of Complaints
### Possible Outcomes
(33)  An investigation will determine that a complaint is not substantiated, partially substantiated, or substantiated. A determination that a complaint is substantiated or partially substantiated may lead to any combination of the following recommendations, or any other outcome deemed appropriate in the circumstances:
  1. rectification of an administrative error;
  2. review of local practices or procedures;
  3. implementation of a negotiated solution;
  4. intervention by an appropriate academic representative;
  5. counselling or training of one, both or all parties;
  6. referral to another process within the University;
  7. referral for disciplinary action, as appropriate (for staff or students);
  8. broader communication to affected cohorts.


### Determination and Implementation of Outcomes
(34)  The relevant school or business area must make a determination regarding the proposed outcome and provide a response to the Student Complaints Office within 10 business days of the complaint being referred to the area.
(35)  Where the responsible person within the Student Complaints Office has any concerns regarding the appropriateness of the proposed outcome they will escalate the matter to the Director, Integrity Office.
(36)  Where a complaint outcome results in a decision or recommendation in favour of the complainant, the relevant school or business area must immediately implement the decision or recommendation and/or take the preventative or corrective action required.
### Communication of Outcomes to Students
(37)  The Student Complaints Office will advise the complainant of the outcome of the complaint in writing within 10 business days of the outcome being finalised and will monitor the implementation of the complaint outcome.
(38)  The outcome letter must be written in clear, everyday English and include:
  1. whether the complaint has been substantiated, partially substantiated or not substantiated;
  2. key activities undertaken during consideration of the complaint (including document review, interviews);
  3. the proposed resolution of the complaint, including actions to be taken and in what timeframe, and the reasons;
  4. information about the complainant’s right to a review of the complaint outcome and how they go about this (see Review section);
  5. the range of support available.


## Part F - Review of Complaint Outcomes
(39)  Complainants who are dissatisfied with any aspect of how this Policy has been applied, or the outcome of their complaint, may seek a review through the Office of the University Ombudsman, under the provisions of the La Trobe University [Ombudsman Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=62). 
(40)  Complainants may also choose to lodge a complaint with an external organisation such as the Australian Human Rights Commission, the Victorian Privacy Commissioner, Victoria Police or the [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated). Some external agencies require that all relevant University complaints processes have been exhausted before they will consider the matter. For further information on complaints considered by the [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated), go to [Making a complaint | National Student Ombudsman (NSO)](https://www.nso.gov.au/making-a-complaint).
(41)  If a complaint is accepted for investigation by an external organisation, the University will normally suspend any in-progress review or University investigation until the external investigation has been completed and all reports submitted.
(42)  The Student Complaints Office may assist complainants to determine whether another organisation can handle the matter more effectively.
## Part G - Withdrawing a Complaint
(43)  A complainant may withdraw a complaint at any time by advising the Student Complaints Office.
(44)  In cases where a complaint has been withdrawn the University retains the right to investigate and address matters raised in that complaint in order to meet its obligations to all students, participants and staff to maintain, as far as is reasonably practicable, a safe and healthy work and study environment. In such instances the confidentiality of the original complainant will be preserved unless this conflicts with the University’s duty of care obligations, or obligations required by law.
(45)  The University makes no undertaking to expunge any records of withdrawn complaints.
## Part H - Recording and Reporting of Complaints
(46)  The University records all formal complaints in accordance with the requirements of the HESF, the [National Code of Practice for Providers of Education and Training to Overseas Students 2018](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=402&version=1&associated) and the University’s [Records Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=10). Complaints lodged in the [SCM](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=60&version=4&associated) are recorded within the system.
(47)  The University assures itself that La Trobe and its third party partners are meeting their obligations in the management of student complaints through the submission and scrutiny of a report every six (6) months by the Student Complaints Office via Education Committee. The report includes:
  1. a summary of complaints received during the previous six (6) months and an analysis of trends from previous periods;
  2. information on the quality and timeliness of complaint handling;
  3. identification of serious complaints and systemic issues, including underlying causes;
  4. information concerning procedural or other changes that may have been made in response to complaints and any actions taken and planned;
  5. measures taken to address any issues identified with staff wellbeing during the handling of complaints.


(48)  Following endorsement by the Education Committee the six-monthly reports are submitted to Academic Board and then referred to University Council for noting.
(49)  The University Ombudsman submits an annual report to University Council on the activities of the Office of the Ombudsman. The report includes an analysis of contacts, resolution times and a summary of academic and administration issues.
(50)  In addition to the reports to governing bodies the Student Complaints Office conducts other reviews including:
  1. regular surveys of complainants to seek feedback about their experience of the complaints process;
  2. regular consultation with students and their representative bodies on proposed changes to policies, procedures and action plans for complaint handling.


(51)  A summary of the University’s responses to feedback is provided to students/respondents who have engaged in the consultation process.
(52)  In accordance with TEQSA recommendations the University publishes de-identified complaints data annually on its website.
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=160#document-top)
# Section 7 - Definitions
(53)  For the purposes of this Policy and Procedure:
  1. anonymous complaints: where the person making the complaint withholds their name or identity.
  2. complaint: an implied or express statement of dissatisfaction where a response is sought, reasonable to expect, or legally required. Complaints are considered: 
    1. informal, where a student or individual seeks a resolution at the local level;
    2. formal, where a student or individual lodges a complaint through the University’s Student Complaints Management system.
  3. complainant: a person who has made a complaint about an aspect of the University or the University environment.
  4. conflict of interest: interest, involvement or information which may influence or be perceived to influence a person’s ability to make objective recommendations or decisions in investigating a complaint.
  5. exceptional circumstances: those circumstances that are beyond an individual’s control for which there was no opportunity to prepare in advance.
  6. external agencies: agencies outside the University, for example, the Victorian Equal Opportunity and Human Rights Commission, Australian Human Rights Commission, Independent Broad Based Anti-Corruption Commission, [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated) or Victoria Police.
  7. partially substantiated complaint: part of the substance of the complaint is established based on the available evidence, and part is unsubstantiated.
  8. participant: a person registered in a short course run by the University.
  9. Procedural Fairness: a legal concept that is sometimes used interchangeably with natural justice. What is procedurally fair will depend on the circumstances but generally involves: 
    1. the right to be told of allegations in sufficient detail to enable a person to respond. This will not necessarily involve the person being given all information, and some confidential information and original documents may not necessarily be provided;
    2. an opportunity to answer to allegations before any decision is made, including sufficient time to respond;
    3. a requirement that a decision maker is not biased and gives genuine consideration to whatever response is given by a person.
  10. parties to the complaint: University staff members or students who are the subject of a complaint.
  11. staff of the University: academic staff including contract staff, visiting appointments, conjoint appointments and guest lecturers; professional and technical staff (including casual and contract staff); staff of partner institutions teaching La Trobe courses.
  12. substantiated complaint: the substance of the complaint is established based on the available evidence.
  13. university community: all students, staff, visitors to the University, contractors and other workers employed by the University, University tenants and their staff.
  14. unsubstantiated complaint: the substance of the complaint is unable to be established based on the available evidence, or the available evidence disproves the substance of the complaint.
  15. vexatious: where a complaint is made in bad faith to cause harm to an individual.
  16. victimisation: subjecting or threatening to subject another person to any detriment because that person, in good faith, has made a complaint, or supported someone in making a complaint or raising a grievance, or provided information during an investigation of a complaint or grievance.

sections.heading: Section 2 - Purpose
sections.text:
(1)  This Policy and Procedure outlines the process by which student behaviour issues will be managed by La Trobe University (the University).
(2)  Where student behaviour issues are assessed as alleged student misconduct, the process is normally governed by the University’s [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37) (the Statute).
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382#document-top)

sections.heading: Section 3 - Scope
sections.text:
(3)  This Policy applies to all students, including those enrolled in La Trobe courses through third party teaching partners, and short course participants (for ease of reference all are referred to as students in this Policy).
(4)  Students from other institutions who reside in La Trobe student accommodation are bound by the Rules of Residence.
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382#document-top)

sections.heading: Section 5 - Policy Statement
Part A - Reporting a Conduct Concern to Safer Community
Temporary Safety and Investigation Integrity Measures
High-Risk Conduct
Referring General Misconduct to the General Misconduct Officer
sections.text:
(14)  Where the Director, Integrity Office is satisfied there is enough evidence to suggest a prima facie case of general misconduct they may refer the matter to a University General Misconduct Officer.
(15)  In considering whether to refer a matter to a General Misconduct Officer, regard will be had to:
  1. the nature and seriousness of the alleged student conduct issue, for example: 
    1. minor, one-off incidents will generally be managed informally where appropriate and possible; and
    2. sexual harm matters will be referred in accordance with the [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy and Procedure](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337).
  2. whether the matter may be more appropriately assessed or managed by another University process (e.g. the [Complex Conduct Assessment and Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=381)).

sections.heading: Part B - Hearing and Determination by General Misconduct Officer
Opportunity to be Heard
sections.text:
(18)  Prior to being required to respond to an allegation, students will be informed in writing of the following:
  1. the basis upon which there is a reasonable belief that the student may have committed general misconduct;
  2. the possible sanction that may be imposed under the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37);
  3. their ability to respond (in writing, via video conference or in person), noting the date, time and location for any meeting; and
  4. their right to be accompanied by a support person. The support person may be a member of the Student Advocacy service or any person chosen by the student, other than a legal practitioner or person with a law degree.


(19)  In exceptional circumstances (e.g. very serious cases and/or where there are complex evidentiary issues), the General Misconduct Officer may allow a student to have representation. The General Misconduct Officer may also seek advice/support from a suitably qualified person (e.g. they may appoint a lawyer to assist in the hearing).
(20)  Where an oral hearing involves an allegation relating to the safety of any person or sexual harm, the General Misconduct Officer will seek advice from the Director, Integrity Office or other suitably qualified individuals on the appropriate arrangements for conducting the hearing.

sections.heading: Procedural Requirements for General Misconduct Officers
sections.text:
(21)  The procedural requirements are set out in Section 11 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37). In hearing and determining any general misconduct matter, the General Misconduct Officer:
  1. may inform themselves on any matter as they say fit;
  2. is bound by the rules of Procedural Fairness; and
  3. is not bound by the rules of evidence or practices or procedures applicable to courts of record.


(22)  The General Misconduct Officer:
  1. must conduct each hearing with as little formality and technicality, and determine each proceeding with as much speed, as the requirements of the Statute, regulations and a proper consideration of the matter permits; and
  2. subject to the Statute and regulations, may regulate their own procedure.

sections.heading: Outcome
Appeal
sections.text: (24)  The General Misconduct Officer will advise the student as soon as practicable of the outcome and their right of appeal to the University Appeals Committee, describing the requirements prescribed in Section 12 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37) for making such an application.

sections.heading: Part C - Action by the Vice-Chancellor – High Risk Misconduct
sections.text:
(25)  Where the Vice-Chancellor is satisfied that:
  1. a student has engaged in general misconduct of the kind referred to in section 4(c),(e) or (f) of the Statute; or
  2. a student’s conduct otherwise poses a risk of injury or damage to any person or property or to the interests or good reputation of the University,


the Vice-Chancellor may, in accordance with Section 13 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37):
  1. exclude the student from the University or any part or facility of the University indefinitely or for a period determined by the Vice-Chancellor; and/or
  2. suspend or terminate the student’s enrolment.


(26)  The Vice-Chancellor must give written notice of their decision to the student concerned as soon as reasonably practicable. A notice of decision must set out the reasons for the decision.
(27)  If the Vice-Chancellor is reasonably satisfied that it is appropriate or necessary in the circumstances, an exclusion decision may be expressed to take effect immediately and, if so expressed, shall take effect immediately, even if the written notice cannot be given to the student concerned immediately.
(28)  A student must comply with an exclusion decision and a student who fails to comply will breach/commit general misconduct.

sections.heading: Part D - Recording and Reporting of Student Conduct Matters
sections.text:
(29)  The University will record all student conduct matters in accordance with the requirements of the [Higher Education Threshold Standards 2021](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?standard=4), the [National Code of Practice for Providers of Education and Training to Overseas Students 2018](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?code=2) and the University’s [Records Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=10).
(30)  A summary of student conduct matters handled each year is included in the Safer Community and Student Conduct annual report for submission to the Office of the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic).

sections.heading: Part E - Breaches of this Policy
sections.text:
(31)  Where a student has any concerns about the way in which this Policy has been applied (as opposed to an appeal about the outcome that has been determined under the Statute), including any concerns about a breach of confidentiality, they may lodge a complaint with the Office of the University Ombudsman. If their concerns relate to the way in which their issue is handled by the University Ombudsman, they may lodge a complaint with an external organisation such as the Australian Human Rights Commission, Victorian Privacy Commissioner, Victoria Police or [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated). For further information on complaints considered by the [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated), go to [Making a complaint | National Student Ombudsman (NSO)](https://www.nso.gov.au/making-a-complaint).
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382#document-top)

sections.heading: Section 7 - Definitions
sections.text:
(32)  For the purpose of this policy and procedure:
  1. exclusion: means the temporary or permanent prohibition of an individual from accessing any or all University facilities and services or participating in University activities. A temporary prohibition may be for a specific period or until a condition or conditions have been met. Where a student or participant is excluded from a course, short course or subject, their enrolment in the course, short course or subject is cancelled and, where not prevented by the terms of their exclusion, they must reapply for admission.
  2. General Misconduct Officer: a staff member with appropriate skills and experience appointed by the Vice-Chancellor to hear and determine all allegations of general misconduct for students that are referred or reported under the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37).
  3. Procedural Fairness: a legal concept that is sometimes used interchangeable with natural justice. What is procedurally fair will depend on the circumstances. It generally involves: 
    1. the right to be told of allegations to be put to a person in sufficient detail to enable them to respond. This will not necessarily involve the person being given all information, and some confidential information and original documents may not necessarily be provided;
    2. an opportunity to answer to allegations before any decision is made, including sufficient time to respond; and
    3. a requirement that a decision maker is not biased and gives genuine consideration to whatever response is given by a person.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382#document-top)

# Section 5 - Policy Statement
(5)  The University’s values of excellence, inclusiveness, diversity, equity and social justice are reflected in the standards of conduct expected of all students, staff and other members of the University community.
(6)  The standards of conduct expected of students are detailed in a range of instruments, including but not limited to the:
  1. [Student Charter](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=225)
  2. [Student Behaviours Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=60)
  3. [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy and Procedure](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337)
  4. [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37)


(7)  The University aims to address behaviour which falls short of the standards of conduct expected via a process that:
  1. encourages an informative, restorative and/or educative response where possible and appropriate;
  2. is impartial and fair to all parties involved;
  3. is confidential wherever possible and maintains all personal information in accordance with the University's [Privacy Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=1);
  4. is transparent and consistent;
  5. is free from victimisation and reprisal;
  6. is managed within an appropriate period.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382#document-top)
# Section 6 - Procedures
## Part A - Reporting a Conduct Concern to Safer Community
(8)  All student behaviour concerns and allegations of student misconduct should be reported to the University’s Safer Community team (information and contact details are available on the Safer Community [webpage](https://www.latrobe.edu.au/students/support/wellbeing/services/safer-community)). Services provided by Safer Community are available to both staff and students at no cost.
(9)  The initial steps taken by Safer Community will generally include, as appropriate:
  1. triaging, screening and assessing the alleged conduct, including consideration of whether any temporary safety and/or investigation integrity measures should be recommended;
  2. providing information and guidance regarding informal management, including time frames and processes;
  3. providing information and guidance to staff regarding their ability to manage disruptions to classes and examinations in accordance with Section 6 and Section 7 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37);
  4. conducting preliminary enquiries and investigations into the alleged conduct to establish whether, in the opinion of the Director, Integrity Office or their nominee, there is enough evidence to support a finding of student misconduct and referral to a General Misconduct Officer under the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37);
  5. referring individuals to other University processes and/or confidential and free support services (e.g. staff or student wellbeing support/case management, Counselling, AccessAbility).


(10)  Safer Community may assist in the informal management of conduct concerns by, amongst other things, educating, facilitating restorative justice and reinforcing the standards of conduct expected of students.
(11)  Safer Community will advise relevant parties of any decision or outcome within five business days of the conclusion of a matter, and will monitor and ensure the prompt implementation of any actions arising from a decision or outcome.
### Temporary Safety and Investigation Integrity Measures
(12)  Pending investigation of a matter and having regard to the nature of the alleged conduct and potential risks, the Pro Vice-Chancellor (Student Experience and Employability) may:
  1. approve the implementation of temporary health and safety and/or investigation integrity measures, including 
    1. changes to the student’s placement location, class, exam timetable or office location;
    2. a direction to the student that they do not contact a member or members of the University community or discuss a matter under investigation;
    3. any other risk mitigation measures appropriate in the circumstances that are consistent with University legislation and/or any relevant delegation.
  2. recommend to the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) that: 
    1. they prohibit a student temporarily from attending any University campus, facility, including student accommodation, and/or University-managed or approved activity or event (e.g. a student placement, orientation event, excursion, tour or conference);
    2. they approve conditions being placed on the student’s enrolment, for instance that they temporarily transfer to an equivalent online course.


### High-Risk Conduct
(13)  Where a student or situation is considered by the Manager, Safer Community and Student Conduct as being high-risk, they may notify the Police or Security and the Director, Integrity Office who will in turn notify the Pro Vice-Chancellor (Student Experience and Employability). The Pro Vice-Chancellor (Student Experience and Employability) will take action as appropriate for the circumstances. This may include:
  1. convening a Threat Assessment and Management Team (TAMT) under the [Complex Conduct Assessment and Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=381);
  2. notifying the Risk Management Office of a Critical Incident and/or the relevant Senior Executive Group (SEG) member;
  3. recommending the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) refer the matter directly to the Vice-Chancellor under Section 13 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37).


### Referring General Misconduct to the General Misconduct Officer
(14)  Where the Director, Integrity Office is satisfied there is enough evidence to suggest a prima facie case of general misconduct they may refer the matter to a University General Misconduct Officer.
(15)  In considering whether to refer a matter to a General Misconduct Officer, regard will be had to:
  1. the nature and seriousness of the alleged student conduct issue, for example: 
    1. minor, one-off incidents will generally be managed informally where appropriate and possible; and
    2. sexual harm matters will be referred in accordance with the [Sexual Harm Prevention and Response Policy and Procedure](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=337).
  2. whether the matter may be more appropriately assessed or managed by another University process (e.g. the [Complex Conduct Assessment and Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=381)).


## Part B - Hearing and Determination by General Misconduct Officer
(16)  The Office of Integrity and Investigations provides support and assistance to General Misconduct Officers, who will hear and determine alleged general misconduct.
(17)  The General Misconduct Officer may:
  1. dismiss the referral and take no further action (e.g., if the alleged conduct does not constitute general misconduct or there is insufficient evidence to support such a finding);
  2. refer the matter to Safer Community for informal resolution;
  3. seek further information and, in complex cases, may approve the appointment of a specialist investigator;
  4. provide the student alleged to have committed general misconduct an opportunity to respond before making a finding as to whether general misconduct has occurred and what sanction, if any, may be appropriate in the circumstances; and/or
  5. take any other reasonable action appropriate in all the circumstances.


### Opportunity to be Heard
(18)  Prior to being required to respond to an allegation, students will be informed in writing of the following:
  1. the basis upon which there is a reasonable belief that the student may have committed general misconduct;
  2. the possible sanction that may be imposed under the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37);
  3. their ability to respond (in writing, via video conference or in person), noting the date, time and location for any meeting; and
  4. their right to be accompanied by a support person. The support person may be a member of the Student Advocacy service or any person chosen by the student, other than a legal practitioner or person with a law degree.


(19)  In exceptional circumstances (e.g. very serious cases and/or where there are complex evidentiary issues), the General Misconduct Officer may allow a student to have representation. The General Misconduct Officer may also seek advice/support from a suitably qualified person (e.g. they may appoint a lawyer to assist in the hearing).
(20)  Where an oral hearing involves an allegation relating to the safety of any person or sexual harm, the General Misconduct Officer will seek advice from the Director, Integrity Office or other suitably qualified individuals on the appropriate arrangements for conducting the hearing.
### Procedural Requirements for General Misconduct Officers
(21)  The procedural requirements are set out in Section 11 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37). In hearing and determining any general misconduct matter, the General Misconduct Officer:
  1. may inform themselves on any matter as they say fit;
  2. is bound by the rules of Procedural Fairness; and
  3. is not bound by the rules of evidence or practices or procedures applicable to courts of record.


(22)  The General Misconduct Officer:
  1. must conduct each hearing with as little formality and technicality, and determine each proceeding with as much speed, as the requirements of the Statute, regulations and a proper consideration of the matter permits; and
  2. subject to the Statute and regulations, may regulate their own procedure.


### Outcome
(23)  Once the General Misconduct Officer has heard from the student, the General Misconduct Officer may:
  1. determine that the alleged general misconduct cannot be substantiated on the available evidence and take no further action;
  2. refer the matter back to the Office of Integrity and Investigations for further inquiries to be conducted;
  3. determine that the alleged misconduct can be substantiated setting out the reasons for the determination and any sanction to be imposed under the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37); or
  4. refer the matter to another University process.


### Appeal
(24)  The General Misconduct Officer will advise the student as soon as practicable of the outcome and their right of appeal to the University Appeals Committee, describing the requirements prescribed in Section 12 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37) for making such an application.
## Part C - Action by the Vice-Chancellor – High Risk Misconduct
(25)  Where the Vice-Chancellor is satisfied that:
  1. a student has engaged in general misconduct of the kind referred to in section 4(c),(e) or (f) of the Statute; or
  2. a student’s conduct otherwise poses a risk of injury or damage to any person or property or to the interests or good reputation of the University,


the Vice-Chancellor may, in accordance with Section 13 of the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37):
  1. exclude the student from the University or any part or facility of the University indefinitely or for a period determined by the Vice-Chancellor; and/or
  2. suspend or terminate the student’s enrolment.


(26)  The Vice-Chancellor must give written notice of their decision to the student concerned as soon as reasonably practicable. A notice of decision must set out the reasons for the decision.
(27)  If the Vice-Chancellor is reasonably satisfied that it is appropriate or necessary in the circumstances, an exclusion decision may be expressed to take effect immediately and, if so expressed, shall take effect immediately, even if the written notice cannot be given to the student concerned immediately.
(28)  A student must comply with an exclusion decision and a student who fails to comply will breach/commit general misconduct.
## Part D - Recording and Reporting of Student Conduct Matters
(29)  The University will record all student conduct matters in accordance with the requirements of the [Higher Education Threshold Standards 2021](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?standard=4), the [National Code of Practice for Providers of Education and Training to Overseas Students 2018](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?code=2) and the University’s [Records Management Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=10).
(30)  A summary of student conduct matters handled each year is included in the Safer Community and Student Conduct annual report for submission to the Office of the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic).
## Part E - Breaches of this Policy
(31)  Where a student has any concerns about the way in which this Policy has been applied (as opposed to an appeal about the outcome that has been determined under the Statute), including any concerns about a breach of confidentiality, they may lodge a complaint with the Office of the University Ombudsman. If their concerns relate to the way in which their issue is handled by the University Ombudsman, they may lodge a complaint with an external organisation such as the Australian Human Rights Commission, Victorian Privacy Commissioner, Victoria Police or [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated). For further information on complaints considered by the [National Student Ombudsman](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/download.php?id=462&version=1&associated), go to [Making a complaint | National Student Ombudsman (NSO)](https://www.nso.gov.au/making-a-complaint).
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382#document-top)
# Section 7 - Definitions
(32)  For the purpose of this policy and procedure:
  1. exclusion: means the temporary or permanent prohibition of an individual from accessing any or all University facilities and services or participating in University activities. A temporary prohibition may be for a specific period or until a condition or conditions have been met. Where a student or participant is excluded from a course, short course or subject, their enrolment in the course, short course or subject is cancelled and, where not prevented by the terms of their exclusion, they must reapply for admission.
  2. General Misconduct Officer: a staff member with appropriate skills and experience appointed by the Vice-Chancellor to hear and determine all allegations of general misconduct for students that are referred or reported under the [General Misconduct Statute 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=37).
  3. Procedural Fairness: a legal concept that is sometimes used interchangeable with natural justice. What is procedurally fair will depend on the circumstances. It generally involves: 
    1. the right to be told of allegations to be put to a person in sufficient detail to enable them to respond. This will not necessarily involve the person being given all information, and some confidential information and original documents may not necessarily be provided;
    2. an opportunity to answer to allegations before any decision is made, including sufficient time to respond; and
    3. a requirement that a decision maker is not biased and gives genuine consideration to whatever response is given by a person.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=382#document-top)
# Section 8 - Authority and Associated Information
(33)  This Policy is made under the [La Trobe University Act 2009](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=8).

sections.heading: Section 5 - Policy Statement
sections.text:
(4)  All fees and charges levied by the University for all student cohorts are managed in compliance with the requirements of relevant Government and University Legislation.
(5)  Tuition fees must not include fees for facilities, goods or services of a non-academic nature.
(6)  The University conducts an annual review of fees and charges, including tuition fees and SSAF, and the application of special circumstances, taking account of any grandparenting arrangements or change in government legislation. Any fee increases will take effect from 1 January in the following calendar year.
(7)  When determining the indexation of fees and charges, the University considers the impact of any increase on continuing students and sets fees relative to the cost and delivery of services.
(8)  The University ensures information regarding student fees (both prospective and current) is accurate and published in a timely manner on the relevant University course pages, that all students are advised of potential for changes in fees and charges during their studies, and that administration processes are consistent with published information. No tuition fees are to be published unless they have been approved by the University Council.
(9)  The University will not market the availability of or misrepresent the conditions by which government fee assistance is applied.
(10)  The University reserves the right to refuse a full or partial refund of tuition fees, unless students clearly meet eligibility requirements as outlined in this Policy and related procedures.
(11)  The University acknowledges that, subject to relevant legislation and provisions in this Policy and its associated procedures, all students are entitled to apply for:
  1. a remission of debt where demonstrable and verifiable special circumstances prevent the completion of a subject or course;
  2. a review of a decision not to grant a remission of debt or refund of fees.

# Section 2 - Purpose
(1)  This Policy sets out the principles for the setting of student fees and charges, the collection of fees and charges payments, and the management of refunds, including the remission of debt and fee liability, in accordance with Commonwealth legislation, including the [Higher Education Support Act 2003](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=78), the [Education Services for Overseas Students Act 2000](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?legislation=57) and the [National Code 2018](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/directory/summary.php?code=2).
[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=367#document-top)
# Section 3 - Scope
(2)  This Policy and associated Procedures apply to:
  1. all University award courses, including subjects from award courses studied as Single, Study Abroad or cross-institutional subjects;
  2. enabling courses and microcredentials;
  3. tuition fees, sundry service charges and Student Services and Amenities Fees (SSAF);
  4. all current, former and prospective students including those enrolled in La Trobe award courses through a third party provider, unless specifically exempted (see below).


(3)  This Policy and associated procedures do not apply to:
  1. short courses that are not microcredentials (see [Short Courses Policy](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=403));
  2. students enrolled in subjects or courses delivered in partnership with other education providers where fees are collected by the partner. The fee policies of the partner institution apply to that enrolment.
  3. the setting and administration of Children’s Centre, Library and student residence fees.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=367#document-top)

# Section 5 - Policy Statement
(4)  All fees and charges levied by the University for all student cohorts are managed in compliance with the requirements of relevant Government and University Legislation.
(5)  Tuition fees must not include fees for facilities, goods or services of a non-academic nature.
(6)  The University conducts an annual review of fees and charges, including tuition fees and SSAF, and the application of special circumstances, taking account of any grandparenting arrangements or change in government legislation. Any fee increases will take effect from 1 January in the following calendar year.
(7)  When determining the indexation of fees and charges, the University considers the impact of any increase on continuing students and sets fees relative to the cost and delivery of services.
(8)  The University ensures information regarding student fees (both prospective and current) is accurate and published in a timely manner on the relevant University course pages, that all students are advised of potential for changes in fees and charges during their studies, and that administration processes are consistent with published information. No tuition fees are to be published unless they have been approved by the University Council.
(9)  The University will not market the availability of or misrepresent the conditions by which government fee assistance is applied.
(10)  The University reserves the right to refuse a full or partial refund of tuition fees, unless students clearly meet eligibility requirements as outlined in this Policy and related procedures.
(11)  The University acknowledges that, subject to relevant legislation and provisions in this Policy and its associated procedures, all students are entitled to apply for:
  1. a remission of debt where demonstrable and verifiable special circumstances prevent the completion of a subject or course;
  2. a review of a decision not to grant a remission of debt or refund of fees.

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=367#document-top)
# Section 6 - Procedures
(12)  The following procedures form part of this Policy suite:
  1. [Student Fees Procedure - Fees Payable](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=405)
  2. [Student Fees Procedure - Refunds](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=404)
  3. [Student Fees Procedure - Remission of Debt or Fee Liability](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=419)

[Top of Page](https://policies.latrobe.edu.au/document/view.php?id=367#document-top)
# Section 7 - Definitions
(13)  For the purpose of this Policy:
  1. charge: all fees for facilities, goods or services, excluding tuition fees and SSAF;
  2. continuing student: a student currently undertaking a course of study at La Trobe University who has completed at least one teaching period of study and who is eligible to continue into a subsequent teaching period;
  3. course: a program of study leading to the award of a degree, diploma, or other award;
  4. enrolment: the process by which a person becomes a student of a subject from or subjects within a course at La Trobe University;
  5. grandparenting: the legal mechanism used by the Commonwealth Government to ensure that the funding and fee charging conditions that students had at the commencement of their program are maintained during the period of their enrolment;
  6. international student: a student who is not a domestic student at the time of the relevant study, and who holds a visa with rights to study in Australia;
  7. partial refund: the balance of fees payable to a student where, dependent on the refund circumstances, the University retains a percentage of ‘fees payable’;
  8. remission of fee liability: cancellation of a student’s liability, incurred at the Census Date, to pay tuition fees upfront to the University, or in the case of Commonwealth-Supported Places (CSP), the Student Contribution Amount;
  9. Student Contribution Amount: based on the band of units a student is enrolled in, the remaining cost of a course after the government subsidy for Commonwealth supported places (CSPs) is applied;
  10. Student Services and Amenities Fee (SSAF): a mandatory contribution fee payable by students to a higher education provider for the establishment and provision of amenities, facilities, and support services of a non-academic and non-political nature;
  11. Study Abroad: a program in which students (incoming or outgoing) enrol in one or more subjects with a higher education institution or third party provider overseas, normally for one semester and for credit towards their course at their home institution. Tuition fees are payable at the host institution, unless the enrolment occurs under an exchange agreement in which case students are only liable for fees payable at their home institution.
  12. subject: a unit of study involving students in a series of learning activities, the outcomes of which are assessed;
  13. third party provider: an external educational institution that teaches La Trobe subjects or courses under a formal agreement with the University. Students under these agreements are enrolled as La Trobe students.
  14. tuition fees: course or subject fees payable by students who are not enrolled in a Commonwealth-Supported Place, including for Single Subjects.
